questions.cardText:
[History] Where and during which dynasty was the first known paper money used?
A. Japan, Edo period
B. India, Gupta Dynasty
C. China, Tang and Song Dynasties
Answer: C. Before the invention of money, trade was conducted through a barter system, where goods and services were exchanged directly. The introduction of banknotes made trade easier and more efficient, eventually leading to the complex financial systems we have today.
questions.de: Unter welcher chinesischen Dynastie entstand der Jiaozi, der als erstes Papiergeld gilt?
questions.en: Under which Chinese dynasty did the jiaozi, regarded as the first paper money, appear?

timeline.labelEn: The Song government issues jiaozi, regarded as the first paper money
timeline.labelDe: Die Song-Regierung gibt Jiaozi aus, das als erstes Papiergeld gilt

questions.notes: Card says 'Tang and Song': the Tang dynasty's 'flying cash' (c. 804) was a negotiable instrument and precursor (Wikipedia: Flying cash), but numismatists regard the Song jiaozi (Sichuan, 11th century) as the first paper money. 1023 = the Song government issue.

questions.cardText:
[Finance] Approximately, what is the unadjusted historic annualized average return of the S&P 500?
A. 5% B. 7% C. 10%
Answer: C. At an average annual return of 10%, a $100 investment would grow to approximately $259 over 10 years due to the power of compounding.
questions.de: Wie hoch war die historische annualisierte Rendite des S&P 500 ungefähr, einschließlich Dividenden und nicht inflationsbereinigt?
questions.en: Approximately what has the historic annualized return of the S&P 500 been, including dividends and not adjusted for inflation?

timeline.labelEn: The S&P 500 index is expanded to 500 companies and given its current name
timeline.labelDe: Der Index S&P 500 wird auf 500 Unternehmen erweitert und erhält seinen heutigen Namen

questions.notes: Wikipedia: compound annual growth rate since 1926, including dividends, about 9.8% (about 6% after inflation) — the card's ~10%. The card's compounding example checks out (1.1^10 ≈ 2.59).
